''The Future Is Today!"
/V.S we approach the �.45th Convention
to be held here in Washington at the
Hyatt Arlington from August 25-28, 1988,
it is time once again to think about the
issues with which our Fraternity must
grapple. Today, it is a cliche to talk about
drug and alcohol abuse, sexual abuse (in
cluding date rape), the threat of AIDS to
all segments of our population, the ob
vious detriments of hazing and its unin
tended results, and the overwhelming
need for risk management in all of these
areas! These are the elements of concern
on a day-to-day basis that lie at the very
heart of our survival as a fraternity sys
tem in a modern world. The newspapers
today are unfortunately full of stories
about one aw^ful "accident" after another
concerning a fraternity chapter or indi
vidual brother who suffers a terrible trag
edy relating to one of the hazards noted
above.
For many, these may simply seem to
be the random misfortunes that one can
expect in an increasingly complex soci
ety. For those of us who have bad an
opportunity to watch the developments
in the fraternity world in the last several
decades, however, it is unfortunately far
more serious than simply happenstance.
These events, each distinct and unique
in its own right, form a pattern that should
be of significant concern to all of us who
believe that the college fraternity pro
vides a unique opportunity for under
graduate bothers to enlarge upon their
undergraduate educational experience
through the unique living experience and
preparation for the future that member
ship in a fraternity can provide.
Let there be no doubt about it �
fra
ternities today are much closer to the
brink of disaster than our numbers would
otherwise indicate. Yes, the number of
fraternity members and fraternity chap
ters have never been higher. Yes, the
number of campuses that have Greek
systems is larger than ever before. Yes,
we
may have "turned the comer" in our
battle to obtain rational liability insur
ance coverage following the "liability cri
sis" that saw insurance premiums soar
beyond reach or disappear altogether
during the 1985-1987 period. But we must
not fool ourselves into beheving that we
can ever return to the "halcyon days" of
the 1930's to the 1960's when alcohol and
hazing were perhaps the norm rather than
the exception. The news events of today
�
the recent Rutgers death, the elimi
nation of fraternities at Amherst, Colby,
and Franklin and Marshall Colleges and
the consideration of such action else
where, the stories of multimillion dollar
lawsuits filed against individual brothers,
chapters, alumni organizations, and na
tional and international fraternities and
their leaders �
are testimony to the fact
that numbers are not the only measure
of success or indeed survival.
The difficulties that our chapters face
are not different than those faced by other
fraternities �
a drinking age that has been
raised to 21 in most states, making illegal
again an activity that for a time had been
legal for most of our undergraduate
members; eliminating hazing practices
that, even when ostensibly eliminated by
one generation of highly-motivated chap
ter leaders, are recreated and become a
"tradition" in another generation, often
encouraged or even enlarged upon by
alumni "who remember when it was really
tough to be initiated into the Y Chapter";
finding ways to educate our members
about how to deal with individual alcohol
and drug abuse problems that have the
potential to ruin their later lives; and pro
viding the necessary incentives and as
sistance to assure the basic maintenance
of our chapter houses in a condition that
is both livable and avoids the traditional
liability problems that plague every con
ceivable living accommodation in the
country.
These are not new problems, but they
are most assuredly more pressing with
each passing year as fraternity houses get
older, as laws become more restrictive,
as litigation becomes more rampant and
the results of such litigation more diffi
cult, and as colleges and universities re
view with greater intensity the contri
bution that fraternities make to the
educational experience of today's under
graduates. All of these factors make our
responsibilities as
fraternity leaders more
critical than ever before �
we must make
bard decisions that mean "tough broth
erhood" to continue to make available to
future generations of undergraduates the
opportunities that were available to us.
These hard decisions include estabhshing meaningful and enforceable policies
about alcohol in fraternity houses and at
fraternity functions, about providing ap
propriate insurance protection against the
risks that exist in our system, and to as
sure that we are doing everything pos
sible to manage these risks to limit our
exposure to liability in a responsible
manner.
Some of these hard decisions will be
presented at the upcoming Convention,
along with a variety of the very positive
steps that are being taken to provide
greater assistance to our chapters �
longawaited guidance for chapter officers to
provide continuity in the performance of
their duties, new rituals to add to the
constructive aspects of the Fraternity
Education Program that emphasize the
long and meaningful history of the Fra
ternity and the strong educational role
that our Fraternity has always had on the
campuses where we exist, and further
exploration of campuses where we do not
have chapters but which lend themselves
to an atmosphere in which Psi U can not
only thrive but provide a real contribu
tion to the educational environment.
Come to Washington and join us in this
continuing search for answers to the tough
questions that face the fraternity system!
The answers must be found today in or
der for us to assure that we will continue
to be an
integral part of the/i^twre on our
respective campuses. And, you can be
sure, we will enjoy ourselves as we de
liberate, renew old acquaintances, and
make new friends!
Yours in the Bonds,
William R. Robie, Epsilon Omega '66

SOMETHING'S BREWING NEAR
CAPITOL HILL
(Arlington, VA) D.C. is astir these days
�
and not only on the political front �
as Psi U's, young and old alike, begin to
gather steam in anticipation of this sum
mer's 145th Convention at the Hyatt Ar
lington. To set the stage for the affair,
the Hyatt hosted a cocktail reception for
D.C. area alumni on May 11. "Fantasy
Island" seemed to be the theme of the
evening as guests were treated to leis,
Hawaiian decorations, and an array ofhors
d'oeuvres that included tropical fruits,
sate, and sushi. Rich Carlson, Epsilon Nu
'69, manager of the Hyatt and host of the
evening's reception, did a wonderful job
of playing Ricardo Montalban for the
night, although no "Smiles, everyone!"
coaxing was
necessary.
After the last toy umbrella had been
cleared away and a final tally taken, over
fifty brothers ranging in class from 1928
to 1987 and representing twenty-five
chapters had attended. A number of our
more prominent Psi U's in Congress and
the State Department also came for the
evening to renew those fraternal bonds.
With such enthusiasm, this summer's
gathering certainly looks promising.
The event was the brainchild of Dick
Dadey, Pi '80, who coordinated all plans
for the evening. The reception not only
stirred up some excitement for the Con
vention but also tested the waters of the
Potomac for Psi U's interested in organ
izing a D.C. area alumni association. The
response was
overwhelmingly positive,
which prompted the first organizational
meeting of interested D.C. area alumni
on June 29.
ZETA ZETA IS ALL-CANADA
(Vancouver, BC) Greg Williscroft, Zeta
Zeta '90, power hitter for the University
of British Columbia Thunderbirds, was
recently named to the All-Canada second
team in volleyball. Williscroft's stellar
performances have led the Thunderbirds
to wins over NCAA powerhouse, the
University of Hawaii, and the 1987 NCAA
champion, UCLA. Against Hawaii, Greg
had 18 kills, one block, and ten digs, and
in competition with the Bruins he pro
duced an amazing 26 winners. If Brother
Wilhscrolt's performances continue at this
level, we may one day see him playing
for the Canadian National Team.
SEOUL BOUND?
(Houston, TX) Also in the sporting news
is Andrew Parkinson, Xi '80, who is an
Olympic hopeful in the increasingly pop
ular sport of boardsailing. With a number
of wins in recent boardsailing champi
onships. Brother Parkinson received an
invitation to serve as one of only eight
boardsailors to participate in the 1986
Olympic sports festival in Houston and a
spot on the U.S. Olympic team. It is not
surprising that he was prompted to leave
his job with Kraft in January of 1987 to
devote his energies to training for this
summer's Games in Seoul.
TWO TIMES RUNNING
(Paoli, PA) For the second straight year,
John B. Dunn, Chi '89, has submitted
the winning convention logo design. This
year's version portrays the "owl of old Psi
U" situated within a diamond and adja
cent to the United States flag (see page
12). Brother Dunn's outstanding art work
will be featured on many of the materials
used at the 145th Convention to be held
August 25-28 in Washington, DC. John,
who hails from Seattle, is an architecture
student at Cornell.

POSTHUMOUS RECOGNITION
(Seattle, WA) Russell S. Callow, Theta
Theta '16, who died in 1961 after an il
lustrious career as a crew coach, has been
selected to the Centennial Hall of Honor
of the State of Washington. In 1989
Washington will celebrate one hundred
years of statehood, and the Washington
State Historical Society is selecting one
hundred people to be honored for ex
ceptional service to the state and nation
during its first one hundred years. "Rusty"
Callow joins this elite group.
Brother Callow coached crew at the
University of Washington from 1922 to
1926, spent twenty-five years coaching at
the University of Pennsylvania, and ended
bis career in 1959 after serving eight years
at the U.S. Naval Academy. His 1952
Navy crew placed first in the Olympic
Games at Helsinki.
Psi Upsilon is extraordinarily fortunate
to count not only "Rusty" Callow among
its ovwi, but also his two sons �
Gordon,
a retired regional chief administrative
judge for the Social Security Administra
tion, and Keith, a justice on the Wash
ington State Supreme Court.

FOUNDATION AWARDS 37
SCHOLARSHIPS FOR 1988-89
It is with great pride and pleasure that The Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc. presents the worthy recipients of 1988-89
scholarship grants. Representing twenty-four chapters, the thirty-seven deserving recipients (chosen from the largest
pool of applicants ever) have been awarded grants totaling $33,050.
The Foundation has undertaken numerous worthwhile projects in recent years, but none is quite so rewarding as
providing hnancial assistance to deserving undergraduates for the purpose ofassisting them in their educational pursuits.
From very modest beginnings, the scholarship program has grown dramatically both in the number of grants and the
amount of each award (see chart below).
A comprehensive application and review procedure is followed each year to identify the most qualified undergrad
uates to receive the awards. A scholarship committee composed of Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39, Chairman; Travis B.
Jacobs, Lambda '62; R. Timothy Leedy, Phi '57; and George T. Sewall, Kappa '32, works diligently each year to
determine the best candidates from the many qualified applicants. Their work has been a major factor in the great
success of this program.
Congratulations to the worthy recipients, all of whom personify the qualities sought in applicants: unquestioned
integrity and strength of character, sound academic standing, participation and leadership in campus activities, and
willingness to accept responsibility in chapter affairs.

WHAT IS A PSI UPSILON CONVENTION?
The Convention is the legislative body of the frater
nity. Delegates from each undergraduate chapter and
alumni association travel from all over the United States
and Canada to meet annually to discuss and take action
on the important issues facing the fraternity in the year
ahead. In addition, a significant portion of Convention
time is devoted to educational sessions on such topics as
alumni relations, social programming, hazing, etc. This
year's schedule also includes special presentations by two
nationally recognized authorities, one on Thursday eve
ning on values and ethics and the other on Friday morn
ing on AIDS. The Executive Council, the administrative
arm of the fraternity, w^ill be holding its summer meeting
during the Convention, as vwll the Alumni Advisory Board
and the Undergraduate Advisory Board.
WHY WASHINGTON, D.C?
Actually, the Convention is being held this year in
Arlington, Virginia, which is somewhat of a departure
from the custom of a chapter hosting the annual event
on its campus. Washington, D.C. was chosen for several
reasons, not the least of which is the large contingent of
Psi U alumni living in the D.C. area who might have
the opportunity to attend their first convention (or their
first in many years). The Hyatt Arlington in Rosslyn,
Virginia, will be the site of all activities. Among its many
advantages are its excellent location (close proximity to
Georgetown and a Metro stop), relatively small size (a

100-person convention like ours can get lost in some of
the very large hotel/convention centers), superb meeting
and dining facilities, and, perhaps most importantly, as
surance of high quality service from its general manager,
Rich Carlson, Epsilon Nu '69.
WHAT EVENTS WILL BE OF PARTICULAR
INTEREST OR ENJOYMENT?
The Phi Beta Chapter at the College of William and
Mary (the closest chapter geographically to Washington,
D.C.) will be hosting a reception Thursday evening at
which attendees will enjoy a taste of Williamsburg. Fri
day's activities will feature a bus tour of the D.C. area
and some free time to explore the nation's capital. The
banquet and dessert reception should ensure a very spe
cial Saturday evening, and Sunday morning's awards
brunch should prove to be an appropriate climax to the
Convention's activities.
All of this information accurately describes the details
of the I45th Convention. But it cannot describe the "in
tangibles." The Convention is a time for old and young
to work together. It is a time to make or renew friend
ships. It is a time to share, to learn, to reminisce, to
laugh, to plan, and to grow. It is a time of brotherhood.

OMICRON CHAPTER HOUSE
UNIVERSITY OF ILLINOIS
JL he magnificent Omicron chapter
house was designed by Benjamin H.
Marshall, noted Chicago architect, in
1924. THE DIAMOND of Novem
ber 1924 describes the Omicron's new
home in this way;
Located on the southwest corner
of Fourth Street and Armory Ave
nue, it is placed on the lot with its
quarter circle facade facing the cor
ner so that the front, east and north
walls combine to make the principal
elevation, and the long front so pro
duced combines pleasingly with the
great elm on the corner as seen from
the principal approach .
As you approach the house, you
see a broad expanse of lawn with the
building set well hackfrom the street
and planted so as to force entrance
well back from the corner on either
street .
The mass and outline of the build
ing develop a natural, rather than
contrived, picturesqueness . The style
shows the same spirit which ani
mated the Sixteenth Century Eng
lishman, when he built in native style
and period [the Omicron chapter
house purportedly was fashioned
after a manor house in Lincolnshire,
England] .
Precisely the same careful
attention to line and proportion, and
right adaptation offeatures to their
purposes are apparent throughout
the building.
The front is dominated by two large
chimneys and centered between them
on the axis ofthe lot and circle is the
main entrance of stone.
Thisfeature rises to a height above
the second story window sills, where
it is topped by the Ancient Owl, and
because it is symbolic, it becomes the
main feature of the building .
The materials used for the walls
are a rough textured brick which will
be treated with a special whitewash .
The window lintels are of stone, as
are also the porch piers of the living
porch on the south.
Entering the house through the
vestibule, you enter a circular gal
lery room from which easy oak stairs
rise to the second floor. The gallery
is treated with heavy wooden beams
and openings cased with heavy tim
bers, framed and nail-studded in ike
English manner. Flanking the main
entrance doors two recesses are
formed and the space thus obtained
is occupied by upholstered seats.
Opening naturally from each end
of the gallery are the living room on
the east and the dining room, on the
north . These roomys are alike in size
and similar in treatment, with rough
plastered walls, brick fireplaces,
brick and masonry window open
ings. The great recessed fireplace in
the living room occupies more than
half of the north wall of this room.
Recesses formed in walls provide
space for chests and the display of
various trophies.
These rooms with the galleryform
practically one room for purposes of
entertaining. To the south of the liv
ing room are a glazed living porch
and a library .
On the south wall of the gallery
and east ofthe main stair a door opens
into a large coat room., in which are
located telephone booths, coat racks,
a lavatory and a drinking fountain:
from, the coat room a stair leads to a
segregated portion of the basement
where are located an anteroom and
an interestingly formed chapter
room.
Half way up the main stairway to
the second floor you enter a guest
room with bathroom and closet, for
use as a cloak room for the ladies at
fraternityfunctions,
and a guest bed
room as occasion offers.
The second floor has twelve study
rooms, each with two closets and each
designedfor the use oftwo men. The
main hall on the second floor con
nects with a south hall and rear stair,
and to the left with a main stair to
the third floor. Here slightly above
the second floor is located the prin
cipal toilet room, a large light room
with tile floor and the most sanitary
fixtures obtainable. Adjoining the
toilet room is a shower room with
four showers. This room is sepa
rately ventilated in order to avoid the

This description of the Omicron
chapter house still holds true today.
Little has changed in the sixty-four
years of occupancy at 313 East Ar
mory Avenue. The only substantive
changes have been renovations to the
basement, surface changes to the
walls, floors, etc., and the replace
ment of outdated mechanical equip
ment.
As with any venerable building in
habited by young men with active
imaginations, the Omicron chapter
house has developed a considerable
body of legend around it: Was the
house really modelled after an Eng
lish manor house, or was it a royal
Scottish hunting lodge? Just where
exactly is the propeller, salvaged from
a plane wreck in the backyard, hid
den within her walls? Who was the
"ghost of the Beta Chi" in life, and
why won't the chapter's cooks ven
ture to the kitchen storeroom after
dark? Just why is there a small (5' X
5') room, complete with radiator, be
neath the dining room? These ques
tions have remained unanswered to
this day.
The Omicron house is certainly not
short of interesting names for its
rooms, either. The most 'colorfiil' of
these is the Red Room. While it has
changed location over the decades,
the spirit remains. In recent years
the basement of the house has been
known as the "Beta Chi" (for base
ment chapter). This fraternity within
a fraternity has long served to con
fuse many people.
Other named areas of the chapter
house include: the halfway house,
which was once a guest room; the
penthouse, which was once a trunk
storage room; and the '28 room, the
library named for one ofthe chapter's
17
truly outstanding classes.
Sixty-four years of memories are
stored within the Omicron chapter
house's very unique walls. The bricks
and mortar make it a stately mansion,
but it is the thousands of young men
who have called it "home" that give
it its charm and dignity.

Robert W. Kamm, Delta '39, recently
retired from his position as assistant dean
and director of administrative services at
the University of Tennessee Space In
stitute (UTSl), culminating an impres
sive career that included leadership in
volvement in several projects with
national and international impact.

the National Advisory Committee for
Aeronautics at the Langley Laboratory in
Hampton, Virginia, in 1940 and later
joined the Glenn L. Martin Company in
Baltimore as a senior aerodynamicist. In
1948 he became executive director of the
panel on facilities for the committee on
aeronautics of the research and devel
opment board in the Pentagon, where he
was instrumental in the establishment of
the Arnold Engineering Development
Center (AEDC). In 1951 he was named
special assistant to Maj. Gen. F. O. Car
roll, the first commander of the new
AEDD.
Eight years later he was asked by the
National Aeronautics and Space Admin
istration to become director of the NASA
Western Operations Office in Santa
Monica. With the AEDC firmly estab
lished and growing into what would ul
timately become the free world's largest
complex of aerospace and aeronautical test
facilities. Brother Kamm embarked upon
his "second career" and joined NASA.
The Western Office was the focal point
for the majority of NASA's contracts with
aerospace contractors for the Mercury,
Gemini, and Apollo programs, the three
manned space flight programs that cul
minated in the first manned landing on
the moon in 1969. Brother Kamm di
rected an organization that provided
technical, contractual, legal, fiscal, and
administrative support to aU NASA proj
ects in southern Calffornia.

NASA team during the period of rapid
growth that culminated in the first
